summary: Describes how to run NETCONF inside a Secure Shell (SSH) session by treating it as an SSH subsystem, so configuration traffic gets SSH's authentication and encryption. It was replaced by RFC 6242.

plainLanguage.summary: NETCONF is a way to give a router instructions. This note says to send those instructions through a locked, secret tunnel called SSH, so nobody can listen in or pretend to be you.

questions: how does netconf use ssh subsystem
subtitle: Running network configuration protocol through a secure encrypted channel.

tldr.problem: Network administrators need to securely configure routers and network equipment, but NETCONF was designed to be transport-agnostic without a default secure delivery mechanism.
tldr.mechanism: NETCONF runs as an SSH subsystem, wrapping the XML-based protocol commands inside SSH's authenticated and encrypted session.
tldr.outcome: This RFC was obsoleted by RFC 6242, which clarified and improved the mapping.

today: RFC 4742 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 6242, which provides clarifications and improvements to the NETCONF over SSH mapping.

sections.title: NETCONF and SSH Basics
sections.content:
NETCONF (Network Configuration Protocol) is an XML-based protocol for managing the configuration of network devices. RFC 4721 defines NETCONF as transport-independent, meaning it can run over different underlying protocols. This RFC defines how to run NETCONF over SSH (Secure Shell), one of the most widely used secure communication protocols.

The mapping treats NETCONF as an SSH subsystem, which is a feature of SSH version 2 that lets clients request a named service instead of starting an interactive shell. This approach avoids parsing shell prompts or output noise.
sections.plainLanguage: NETCONF is instructions for routers, and SSH is a secret tunnel. This RFC says how to send the instructions through the tunnel so they stay secret and safe.

sections.title: Establishing a NETCONF over SSH Session
sections.content:
To start a NETCONF session over SSH, a client establishes an SSH transport connection, authenticates the user using SSH's authentication protocol, then opens an SSH channel of type session. Once the SSH session is established, the client invokes the NETCONF subsystem by name.

The RFC requires servers to default to listening on IANA-assigned TCP port 830 for the netconf SSH subsystem, allowing firewalls to easily identify and filter NETCONF traffic. However, servers SHOULD be configurable to allow access over other ports. The client command to invoke the subsystem looks like: ssh -s server.example.org -p 830 netconf
sections.plainLanguage: First you create a secret tunnel (SSH), then you open a door to a service called netconf inside it. This usually happens on port 830 so routers know to expect it.

sections.title: Capabilities Exchange
sections.content:
When a NETCONF session starts, both the server and client immediately send XML documents containing a <hello> element. This hello message advertises the sender's capabilities to the other side. Capabilities describe which NETCONF features the sender supports, such as different data models or optional features.

The special character sequence ]]>]]> terminates each XML document. This sequence cannot legally appear in XML, so it unambiguously marks the document boundary and allows resynchronization if an XML parsing error occurs.
sections.plainLanguage: After connecting, both sides say hello and list what tricks they can do. They use a special sequence to mark where each message ends.

sections.title: Message Exchange and Operations
sections.content:
Once capabilities are exchanged, the client (manager) sends complete XML documents containing <rpc> elements to request operations like <get-config> to retrieve configuration. The server (agent) responds with <rpc-reply> elements containing the result or error. Each request has a message-id attribute so replies can be matched to requests.

For example, a client might send an RPC requesting the running configuration, and the server would reply with the current configuration data wrapped in the reply. Both sides continue this pattern until one sends a <close-session> command to end the NETCONF session, after which the SSH channel closes.
sections.plainLanguage: The client asks questions in special XML tags (RPCs), and the server answers in reply tags. Each message has an ID number so they know which answer goes with which question.

sections.title: Security and Authentication
sections.content:
NETCONF allows reading and modifying network configuration, so access must be restricted to authorized users and systems. Both sides MUST verify and authenticate each other according to local policy before exchanging configuration or state data. The client MUST verify the server's identity, and the server MUST verify the client's identity before allowing access.

SSH provides strong encryption for both authentication and data transfer, protecting sensitive configuration data like usernames and security keys. The default requirement to use TCP port 830 helps firewalls and network devices identify and filter NETCONF traffic, though this also makes it slightly easier for attackers to target. Servers must carefully manage which ports allow NETCONF access to avoid unintended exposure.
sections.plainLanguage: Only trusted people should be able to change router settings. Before letting anyone in, both sides check who they really are. SSH keeps everything secret so nobody can peek or trick anyone.
